messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Nguyen was a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian student who came to treatment after months of feeling as if the danger he had fled had followed him home. Before the trauma, he had volunteered as a relief worker in a war zone, helping distribute supplies and move injured civilians through streets where checkpoints, soldiers, and police were part of the daily landscape. One afternoon, while carrying boxes of food near a heavily guarded compound, he was stopped and questioned by armed men in military uniforms. He remembered the hard stare of a policeman leaning close, the way he felt pinned under being watched, and the sense that any wrong movement could make the situation turn violent in an instant. He had been trying to do something useful, something that mattered, and yet he left with the conviction that he had been helpless and had failed in his most important role in life. From that point on, uniforms, weapons, and the sight of authority figures carried the weight of that day, and even ordinary moments of being observed by strangers in public began to pull him back into the same fear.

In the months that followed, Minh began to organize his life around not encountering those reminders. At university he started choosing empty stairwells, sitting where no one could easily see him, and keeping his head down if a classmate from before the deployment waved at him across campus. He would leave lecture early rather than pass a security guard in a dark jacket, and if he saw police near the student union or a veteran in a military-style uniform on the street, he would cross to the other side or turn back entirely. Even making eye contact felt dangerous; he said it was as if the other person might see through him and notice how unsettled he was. These moments were not just uncomfortable to him—they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe about himself. He was certain his body had betrayed him, that it kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and that meant he could not trust himself to stay steady in the present. The more he noticed his heart racing or his muscles tightening at the sight of a uniform or a watchful face, the more convinced he became that he was fundamentally unsafe and unable to stop bad things from happening to him.

That conviction sharpened the reminders themselves. When Minh felt watched in a classroom, or noticed a police officer standing near the campus entrance, his mind would flash back to the compound, the weapons, the uniforms, the sensation of being trapped under another person’s gaze. Because he believed he had failed when it mattered most, the same scenes seemed to return with even greater force, as if the world were proving him right. He began to anticipate the next moment of scrutiny before it arrived, scanning windows, doorways, and faces for signs that someone was observing him. In that state, ordinary encounters became potent triggers: a professor at the front of the room, a security guard outside the library, a student in a military-style jacket. Each one seemed to announce that he was once again the man who could not protect anyone, and the fear of being seen made him feel as though he were already exposed and powerless.

By the time he sought help, Minh’s world had shrunk considerably. He had fewer friends on campus because he avoided social contact with people he had known before the event, and he often ate alone rather than risk the strain of conversation. His grades had begun to slip because he was late to lectures, left buildings abruptly, and could not concentrate once he had noticed a police car or a uniformed officer nearby. What frightened him most was that the reactions felt automatic and out of his control, as though his body had learned a permanent state of alarm that no amount of telling himself he was back in America could undo. Sitting in the intake appointment, he said he was not only afraid of uniforms or being watched, but of what it meant that these things still had such power over him: that perhaps he had never really left the war behind, and that he might never be able to live as a student, a friend, or simply a young man who could look others in the eye without feeling hunted.
